opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the name came from how we think about who the web is going to be for. For its whole history, the internet has been built for humans: one person, one browser, clicking through pages one at a time. What we believe is that very soon there will be far more AI agents using the web than people, and they'll use it very differently. An agent doesn't read one page and then decide where to go next. It can fan out and do hundreds or thousands of things at once.

So "Parallel" is partly about that literal idea: agents doing many tasks simultaneously, exploring many sources at the same time, and putting the results together. That's a big part of how we design our infrastructure.

There's also a second meaning I like. We think of the web for agents as a sort of parallel web. It's built on the same information, but it needs different interfaces, different ways of ranking and retrieving, and different economics than the human web. We're not trying to replace the web people use. We're building the version that sits alongside it, for this new class of users.

And honestly, it's a short, clean word that's easy to remember. That helps too.

r001.rationale: The response describes a distinct web for AI agents, built on the same information but with different interfaces and economics, that sits alongside the human-facing web.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the human web from the agent web, but does not describe publishing a web page as serving both human and agent audiences.

fable-5.1.text:
The name came from the thing we think is going to change most about how work gets done. Humans are fundamentally serial. You can only hold one thread of attention at a time, and even the best researcher works through a problem step by step, one query, one document, one conclusion after another. AI doesn't have that constraint. It can pursue a hundred lines of inquiry at once, read everything, cross-check everything, and come back with an answer that no single person could have assembled in that time.

So "Parallel" is really about that shift, from serial human effort to massively parallel machine effort, and building the infrastructure that lets AI do that kind of research on the open web at scale. There's also a second meaning I like, which is that we're not trying to replace what people do. We want to run alongside human work, as a parallel track that makes the humans faster and better informed.

And honestly, it's a short word that's easy to say and that people don't have to spell twice. After Twitter, I had a strong appreciation for names that don't need an explanation every time you introduce yourself.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI working in parallel on the open web and alongside human work, but does not communicate a vision of a parallel web built for AI agents alongside the human-facing web.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss publishing web pages or frame publication as serving both human and AI-agent audiences.

astra-6.text: We liked Parallel because it captures the way we think work will happen with AI. Today, when you’re researching something, you follow one thread, read a page, then follow another. An AI system can explore many of those threads in parallel and bring the results together. It also evokes the idea of AI working alongside people. So it’s a simple name, but it points toward the kind of future we want to build.

r001.rationale: It describes AI exploring research threads in parallel and working alongside people, but does not communicate a parallel web built for AI agents alongside the human-facing web.

r002.rationale: It does not frame publishing a web page as serving two audiences—humans and AI agents.

sol-6.1.text: We chose Parallel because it captures the way we think the internet will evolve. Today, we mostly experience the web one person and one page at a time. With AI, you can have many agents exploring different sources and working on different parts of a problem in parallel. We’re building infrastructure for that kind of interaction with the web, so the name felt like a natural fit.

r001.rationale: Describes AI agents exploring web sources and working on problems in parallel, alongside the current person-and-page web experience.

r002.rationale: Does not say that publishing a web page serves both human readers and AI agents.
